author: Khan Academy
description:
Much like a peach, Earth is divided into layers. The thinnest layer is the crust, which composes all the continents and ocean basins. The crust is divided into several massive tectonic plates. Beneath the crust is the mantle, the largest layer. Next is Earth’s outer core, a liquid layer of molten iron and nickel. This spins round the solid inner core, a dense sphere of iron and nickel. The movement of the outer core around the inner core creates Earth’s magnetic field, which protects the planet from harmful solar radiation. 

Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS): MS-ESS2-2, MS-ESS2-3, MS-ESS2.A.2, MS-ESS2.B.1.

description:
Earth’s tides are caused by the gravitational attraction of the Moon and  Earth. This net force creates a tidal bulge that moves across Earth’s oceans, creating predictable cycles of low and high tide. Spring tides and neap tides are caused by particular configurations of the Earth-Sun-Moon system.

author: Khan Academy
description:
There are many misconceptions about what causes the seasons. It’s not the changing distance of Earth to the Sun, but Earth’s axial tilt that causes the seasons. When the Northern Hemisphere is experiencing summer, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun. This causes more direct sunlight to fall on the Northern Hemisphere. Six months later, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. It receives less direct sunlight, and therefore experiences winter. The equinoxes occur midway between the points, when the length of day and night are equal.

Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS): MS-ESS1-1, MS-ESS1.B.

Density is a measure of how much mass is packed into a given volume. This is determined by the mass and number of particles occupying a given space. The relative density of a substance may be used to predict whether it will float on another substance. For instance, anything with a greater density than water sinks in water, but anything with a lower density than water floats on water.

Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS): MS-PS1-2, PS1.A2.

A mixture is a physical combination of two or more different substances. Mixtures can always be separated into their components using physical properties. There are two types of mixtures. Homogeneous mixtures have a uniform appearance throughout. They seem completely blended to the human eye. Homogeneous mixtures are called solutions. In a heterogeneous mixture, the different components have visible boundaries. Mixtures may include any phase of matter. 


Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS): MS-PS1-1, PS1.A1

Physical properties like luster, malleability, and ductility help distinguish the 118 building blocks called elements. These elements are grouped into three categories based on shared characteristics: metals, metalloids, and non-metals. The periodic table organizes these groups in repeating patterns, which helps predict how they behave.
